questions.question:
Consider the given system of linear equations for variables [latex]x[/latex] and [latex]y[/latex], where [latex]k[/latex] is a real-valued constant. Which of the following option(s) is/are CORRECT?

[latex]x + k y = 1[/latex]
[latex]k x + y = -1[/latex]

options.A: There is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the above system of equations has no solution.
options.B: There exist an infinite number of values of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has no solution.
options.C: There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has exactly one solution.
options.D: There exists exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] for which the system of equations has an infinite number of solutions.

questions.explanation:
[latex]\begin{cases}x+ky=1\\kx+y=-1\end{cases}[/latex], with determinant [latex]\Delta=1-k^2[/latex].

No solution requires [latex]\Delta=0[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k=\pm1[/latex]) and the two equations to actually be inconsistent (parallel but not identical lines):
- [latex]k=1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x+y=1[/latex] and [latex]x+y=-1[/latex] — parallel, contradictory → no solution.
- [latex]k=-1[/latex]: equations become [latex]x-y=1[/latex] and [latex]-x+y=-1[/latex], which is just the first equation multiplied by [latex]-1[/latex] — the same line → infinitely many solutions, not "no solution."

So there is exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=1[/latex]) giving no solution, and exactly one value of [latex]k[/latex] (namely [latex]k=-1[/latex]) giving infinitely many solutions. For every other [latex]k[/latex] (i.e. [latex]k\ne\pm1[/latex]), [latex]\Delta\ne0[/latex] and there's a unique solution — but that happens for infinitely many values of [latex]k[/latex], not just one, so the "exactly one k gives a unique solution" claim is false.

Answer: Exactly one k gives no solution; and exactly one k gives infinitely many solutions.

questions.question:
Let [latex]n>1[/latex]. Consider an [latex]n \times n[/latex] matrix [latex]M[/latex] with its elements from [latex]\mathbb{R}[/latex]. Let the vector [latex](0,1,0,0, \ldots, 0) \in \mathbb{R}^{n}[/latex] be in the null space of [latex]M[/latex].
Which of the following options is/are always correct?

options.D: There are at least two non-zero vectors in the null space of [latex]M[/latex]

questions.explanation:
Since [latex](0,1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex] is in the null space of [latex]M[/latex], we have [latex]M\cdot(0,1,0,\ldots,0)^T=\mathbf{0}[/latex]. But [latex]M[/latex] times this unit vector simply extracts the 2nd column of [latex]M[/latex]. So the 2nd column of [latex]M[/latex] is entirely zero.

- Determinant: A matrix with an all-zero column always has determinant [latex]0[/latex]. So "[latex]\det(M)=0[/latex]" is always true. ("[latex]\det(M)=1[/latex]" is always false.)
- Rank: The rank could be anywhere from [latex]0[/latex] to [latex]n-1[/latex] depending on the other columns, so "rank [latex]=1[/latex]" is not always true.
- Null space size: Since the null space contains the nonzero vector [latex](0,1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], it also contains every scalar multiple of it (e.g. [latex](0,2,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], [latex](0,-1,0,\ldots,0)[/latex], etc.), giving infinitely many, hence at least two, distinct non-zero vectors in the null space. This is always true.

Answer: Determinant of M is 0; and there are at least two non-zero vectors in the null space of M.

questions.question:
[latex] A = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 \end{pmatrix}, [/latex]
then which ONE of the following is [latex]A^8 [/latex]?
questions.explanation:
Eigenvalues of [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&-1\end{bmatrix}[/latex]: [latex](1-\lambda)(-1-\lambda)-4=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2-1-4=0\Rightarrow\lambda^2=5\Rightarrow\lambda=\pm\sqrt5[/latex]

Since [latex]A[/latex] is symmetric, it's diagonalizable with these eigenvalues, and [latex]A^8[/latex] has eigenvalues [latex](\sqrt5)^8=5^4=625[/latex] and [latex](-\sqrt5)^8=625[/latex] as well (both eigenvalues raised to an even power give the same positive result). Since both eigenvalues of [latex]A^8[/latex] equal [latex]625[/latex], [latex]A^8[/latex] is simply the scalar matrix [latex]625I[/latex].

Answer: [[625,0],[0,625]]

questions.question:
Consider the function [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex] defined as follows:

[latex] f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{lr} c_{1} e^{x}-c_{2} \log _{{e}}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right), & \text { if } x>0 \\ 3 & \text { otherwise } \end{array}\right. [/latex]

where [latex]c_{1}, c_{2} \in \mathbb{R}[/latex].

If [latex]f[/latex] is continuous at [latex]x=0[/latex], then [latex]c_{1}+c_{2}=[/latex] ________. (answer in integer)
questions.explanation:
For [latex]f[/latex] to be continuous at [latex]x=0[/latex], we need [latex]\lim_{x\to0^{+}}f(x)=f(0)=3[/latex].

[latex]\lim_{x\to0^{+}}\left[c_1e^{x}-c_2\log_e\left(\dfrac1x\right)\right][/latex]

As [latex]x\to0^{+}[/latex]: [latex]e^{x}\to1[/latex], while [latex]\log_e(1/x)=-\log_e x\to+\infty[/latex]. For the overall limit to be a finite number, the coefficient of this diverging term must be zero:
[latex]c_2=0[/latex].

With [latex]c_2=0[/latex], the limit becomes [latex]c_1\cdot1=c_1[/latex]. Setting this equal to [latex]f(0)=3[/latex] gives [latex]c_1=3[/latex].

So [latex]c_1+c_2=3+0=3[/latex].

Answer: 3

questions.question:
Let A and B be two nxn matrices over real numbers. Let rank(M) and det(M) denote the rank and determinant of a matrix M, respectively. Consider the following statements.

I. rank(AB)=rank (A)rank (B)
II. det(AB)=det(A)det(B)
III. rank(A+B) [latex]\leq[/latex] rank (A) + rank (B)
IV. det(A+B) [latex]\leq[/latex] det(A) + det(B)

Which of the above statements are TRUE?
questions.explanation:
Use A = B = I (n = 2):
- I: rank(AB) = 2 but rank(A)rank(B) = 4 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- II: det(AB) = det(A)det(B) is always true [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- III: rank is subadditive: [latex]rank(A+B)\le rank(A)+rank(B)[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- IV: det(2I) = 4 [latex]\gt[/latex] det(I) + det(I) = 2 [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: II and III only

questions.question:
Let [latex]f: \mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}[/latex] be defined as follows:

[latex] f(x)=\left(\frac{|x|}{2}-x\right)\left(x-\frac{|x|}{2}\right) [/latex]

Which of the following statements is/are true?
questions.explanation:
Simplify [latex]f(x)=\left(\dfrac{|x|}{2}-x\right)\left(x-\dfrac{|x|}{2}\right)=-\left(x-\dfrac{|x|}{2}\right)^2[/latex], which is always [latex]\le0[/latex].

- For [latex]x\ge0[/latex]: [latex]|x|=x[/latex], so [latex]f(x)=-\left(\dfrac{x}{2}\right)^2=-\dfrac{x^2}{4}[/latex].
- For [latex]x<0[/latex]: [latex]|x|=-x[/latex], so [latex]f(x)=-\left(\dfrac{3x}{2}\right)^2=-\dfrac{9x^2}{4}[/latex].

Both pieces equal [latex]0[/latex] at [latex]x=0[/latex] and are negative (and decreasing towards [latex]-\infty[/latex]) moving away from [latex]0[/latex] in either direction. So [latex]f[/latex] has a clear local (in fact global) maximum at [latex]x=0[/latex], and since [latex]f\to-\infty[/latex] on both sides with no interior dip, [latex]f[/latex] has no local minimum.

[latex]f'(x)=-x/2[/latex] for [latex]x\ge0[/latex] and [latex]f'(x)=-9x/2[/latex] for [latex]x<0[/latex]. Both pieces approach [latex]0[/latex] as [latex]x\to0[/latex], so [latex]f'[/latex] is continuous everywhere including at [latex]0[/latex]. But the slope of [latex]f'[/latex] jumps from [latex]-1/2[/latex] (just right of [latex]0[/latex]) to [latex]-9/2[/latex] (just left of [latex]0[/latex]), so [latex]f'[/latex] has a corner at [latex]x=0[/latex] and is not differentiable there (hence not differentiable "over [latex]\mathbb R[/latex]").

Answer: f has a local maximum; f' is continuous over R; f' is not differentiable over R.

If the following system has non-trivial solution,
px+qy+rz=0
qx+ry+pz=0
rx+py+qz=0,
then which one of the following options is TRUE?

Non-trivial solution needs determinant = 0:

[latex]\begin{vmatrix}p&q&r\\q&r&p\\r&p&q\end{vmatrix}=-(p+q+r)(p^2+q^2+r^2-pq-qr-rp)=0[/latex]

The second factor is [latex]\frac12[(p-q)^2+(q-r)^2+(r-p)^2][/latex], zero only when p = q = r.

Answer: p + q + r = 0 or p = q = r

questions.question: Let [latex] A [/latex] be any [latex] n \times m [/latex] matrix, where [latex] m > n [/latex]. Which of the following statements is/are TRUE about the system of linear equations [latex] A x=0 [/latex] ?

options.A: There exist at least [latex] m-n [/latex] linearly independent solutions to this system
options.B: There exist [latex] m-n [/latex] linearly independent vectors such that every solution is a linear combination of these vectors
options.C: There exists a non-zero solution in which at least [latex] m-n [/latex] variables are 0
options.D: There exists a solution in which at least [latex] n [/latex] variables are non-zero

questions.explanation:
[latex]rank(A)\le n \lt m[/latex], so the solution space has dimension [latex]m-rank(A)\ge m-n[/latex].

- At least [latex]m-n[/latex] linearly independent solutions [latex]\text{---}[/latex] TRUE.
- "[latex]m-n[/latex] vectors span every solution" fails when the dimension is larger, e.g. A = zero matrix (dimension m) [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=[1\;\;1][/latex] ([latex]n=1,m=2[/latex]): solutions are [latex]t(1,-1)[/latex]; no non-zero solution has a zero entry, though [latex]m-n=1[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.
- [latex]A=\begin{bmatrix}1&0&0\\0&1&0\end{bmatrix}[/latex]: solutions [latex](0,0,t)[/latex] have only 1 non-zero variable [latex]\lt n=2[/latex] [latex]\text{---}[/latex] FALSE.

Answer: There exist at least [latex]m-n[/latex] linearly independent solutions
